questions.question: Mia slides her paper triangle 5 squares to the right across her desk. It does not turn and it does not flip over. Which single transformation is this?
options: Reflection
Translation
Rotation
No transformation
questions.explain: A slide with no turning and no flipping is a translation — the shape keeps its size and still faces the same way. The common trap is calling every move a "flip"; a flip only happens when the shape turns over a mirror line.

questions.question: Leo folds his paper along a line so the line acts like a mirror, then traces his cedar-weave design onto the other side so it faces the opposite way. Which single transformation has he made?
options: Translation
Rotation
Enlargement
Reflection
questions.explain: Folding over a mirror line and copying to the other side is a reflection (a flip). Watch out: a reflection does not make the design bigger or smaller — only its direction changes.

questions.question: A weaver turns her basket design a quarter turn (90°) around a centre point. Which statement names the transformation correctly?
options: Reflection, because the design now faces a new way
Translation, because the design has moved
Rotation, because the design turns about a point
Enlargement, because the design looks different
questions.explain: Turning a shape around a fixed point is a rotation, no matter how far it turns. A reflection would need a mirror line, and a translation would slide the shape without turning it at all.

questions.question: On grid paper, Ravi translates (slides) a woven square shape 6 squares to the right. What is true about the image?
options: It is the same size and still faces the same way
It is the same size but now faces the opposite way
It is smaller than the original shape
It is turned upside down
questions.explain: A translation only changes position — size, shape and direction all stay the same. Students often think sliding a shape also turns or flips it, but only a rotation turns it and only a reflection flips it.

questions.question: Emma marks a bead of her woven star at the point (2, 3) on a grid. She translates the star 4 units right and 2 units down. Where is that bead now?
questions.explain: Right adds to the first number and down subtracts from the second: (2 + 4, 3 − 2) = (6, 1). The usual mistake is adding for "down" instead of subtracting, or writing the two numbers in the wrong order.

questions.question: Noah reflects a cedar-weave shape across a vertical mirror line on his grid paper. One corner of the shape is 3 squares to the left of the mirror line. Where is the matching corner on the image?
options: 6 squares to the right of the line, at the same height
3 squares to the left of the line, at the same height
3 squares to the right of the line, at the same height
3 squares to the right of the line, 3 squares lower
questions.explain: A reflected point sits the same distance from the mirror line, just on the other side — 3 left becomes 3 right, at the same height. A common trap is counting 3 squares past the line from the original point and landing 6 squares away.

questions.question: Jayden turns his square weaving frame a quarter turn (90°) clockwise. A red bead was at the top-left corner before the turn. Which corner is it at now?
options: The bottom-left corner
The top-right corner
The bottom-right corner
It stays at the top-left corner
questions.explain: Clockwise moves each corner to the next corner in the direction the clock hands go, so top-left travels to top-right. Choosing bottom-left means you turned it counterclockwise instead.

questions.question: Ava's woven hat band repeats the same figure across the row. Each figure is 4 cm to the right of the one before it, and every figure leans the same way. Which single transformation takes one figure to the next?
options: A reflection across a vertical mirror line
A rotation of 90° clockwise about a corner
A rotation of 180° about a point between them
A translation of 4 cm to the right
questions.explain: Because every figure still leans the same way, nothing has been turned or flipped — it is a translation of 4 cm right. If it were a reflection, every second figure would lean the opposite way.

questions.question: Priya draws an arrow on grid paper: the tip points right and there is a small notch on the top edge. She reflects the whole arrow across a vertical mirror line. Where are the tip and the notch on the image?
options: The tip points left and the notch is on the bottom
The tip points left and the notch is still on the top
The tip points right and the notch is on the bottom
The tip points up and the notch is on the left
questions.explain: A vertical mirror line swaps left and right only, so the tip flips to the left while the top stays the top. The most common mistake is thinking any flip turns the shape upside down — that would need a horizontal mirror line or a half turn.

questions.question: On Sam's beading loom, one bead moved from (1, 2) to (5, 4) using a single translation. A second bead starts at (3, 6) and is moved by the same translation. Where does the second bead land?
questions.explain: First find the slide: from (1, 2) to (5, 4) is 4 right and 2 up, so (3 + 4, 6 + 2) = (7, 8). The trap is adding the same number to both coordinates, or thinking every bead ends up at the first bead's finishing point.

questions.question: A cedar bark design is a triangle with its long edge along the bottom and its point at the top-left. In the finished weaving, the image of that triangle has its long edge along the top and its point at the bottom-right. Which single transformation takes the design to its image?
options: A translation straight down
A reflection across a horizontal mirror line
A reflection across a vertical mirror line
A half turn (180° rotation) about a point
questions.explain: Check both changes: the point moved from top to bottom AND from left to right, which only a half turn does. A horizontal mirror line would move the point to the bottom but leave it on the left, so it looks right at first glance and is the usual wrong choice.

questions.question: Mei turns her square woven mat a quarter turn clockwise about its centre, three times in a row. Which single transformation would leave the mat in exactly the same final position?
options: A quarter turn counterclockwise about the centre
A half turn about the centre
A reflection across a vertical line through the centre
No transformation, because it is back where it started
questions.explain: Three quarter turns make 90° + 90° + 90° = 270° clockwise, and 270° clockwise lands in the same place as one quarter turn (90°) counterclockwise. Many students assume three turns bring the mat back to the start — it takes four quarter turns to do that.
